title: Take-home Exercise 2 | Urban Bus Mobility Patterns in Singapore
text:
Urban mobility patterns reveal how cities function and evolve. This exercise analyzes bus passenger boarding patterns across Singapore using advanced geospatial statistical methods. By applying Local Measures of Spatial Association (LMSA) and Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA), we identify where passenger demand clusters are located and how they evolve over time during different periods of the week.


Identify spatial clustering patterns in bus passenger boarding volumes across Singapore’s hexagonal traffic analysis zones using Local Moran’s I, Local Geary’s C, and Getis-Ord Gi* statistics.
Detect emerging mobility trends by analyzing how passenger demand hotspots evolve over time – whether they are new, intensifying, diminishing, or sporadic.
Compare mobility patterns across weekday morning peak, weekday afternoon peak, and weekend/holiday periods.


Where are the spatial hotspots and coldspots of bus passenger boarding volumes during weekday morning peak, weekday afternoon peak, and weekend/holiday periods?
How do passenger boarding patterns differ spatially across neighborhoods and planning areas in Singapore?
Are there significant spatial outliers – locations with unusually high or low passenger volumes compared to their surroundings?
How are passenger demand hotspots evolving over time – are they new, intensifying, diminishing, or exhibiting sporadic patterns across the observed period?
What are the implications of these spatial and temporal patterns for public transport planning and urban mobility management?

The summary statistics reveal relatively similar trip patterns across the three time periods.

Weekday morning peak shows the highest maximum value (288,060 trips) and greatest variability (SD = 16,542), indicating more extreme high-volume hexagons.
Weekday afternoon peak records the highest mean (9,769 trips) and median (4,434 trips), suggesting consistently strong activity across hexagons.
Weekend/holiday exhibits lower central tendency (mean = 8,952, median = 3,932) but the highest maximum value (334,516 trips), indicating the presence of exceptional hotspots despite overall lower average demand.

All three periods show substantial standard deviations relative to their means, confirming the right-skewed distributions observed in the histograms. The similar minimum values (1-2 trips) and first quartiles (Q1 ranging 657-1,549) across periods indicate that low-activity hexagons maintain consistently minimal trip generation regardless of time period. The total number of active hexagons is comparable across all periods (2,135-2,152), suggesting stable spatial coverage of bus service demand throughout the week.

title: Take-home Exercise 2 | Urban Bus Mobility Patterns in Singapore
text:
Exploratory Data Analysis
Check for isolated hexagons
This check is crucial for us to decide which package to use: sfdep or spdep, because st_weights() of sfdep package is unable to calculate weights when a polygon has zero neighbors, while poly2nb() of spdep just creates an empty entry for isolated polygons making it possible to calculate metrics e.g. Moran’s I.

Check for isolated hexagons and if they contain bus stopscheck_for_isolated_hexagons <- function(hex_grid, bus_stops) {
  # Create neighbor list
  nb <- poly2nb(hex_grid, queen = TRUE)
  
  # Find isolated hexagons
  n_neighbors <- card(nb)
  isolated <- which(n_neighbors == 0)
  
  if(length(isolated) > 0) {
    cat("Found", length(isolated), "isolated hexagon(s)\n\n")
    
    # Get isolated hexagons
    isolated_hexagons <- hex_grid[isolated, ]
    
    # Check if they contain bus stops using spatial intersection
    bus_stops_in_isolated <- st_intersects(isolated_hexagons, bus_stops)
    
    # Count bus stops in each isolated hexagon
    n_bus_stops <- lengths(bus_stops_in_isolated)
    
    # Create summary table
    isolated_summary <- data.frame(
      HEX_ID = isolated_hexagons$HEX_ID,
      WEEKDAY_MORNING_PEAK = isolated_hexagons$Weekday_Morning_Peak,
      WEEKDAY_AFTERNOON_PEAK = isolated_hexagons$Weekday_Afternoon_Peak,
      WEEKEND_HOLIDAY = isolated_hexagons$Weekend_Holiday,
      N_BUS_STOPS = n_bus_stops
    )
    
    cat("Isolated hexagons summary:\n")
    print(kable(isolated_summary))
    
    # Provide recommendations based on findings
    has_bus_stops <- sum(n_bus_stops > 0)
    
    cat("\n=== ANALYSIS ===\n")
    cat("Isolated hexagons with bus stops:", has_bus_stops, "\n")
    cat("Isolated hexagons without bus stops:", length(isolated) - has_bus_stops, "\n")
    
    cat("\n=== RECOMMENDATION ===\n")
    if(has_bus_stops > 0) {
      cat("✓ Some isolated hexagons contain bus stops and have trip data\n")
      cat("✓ Use spdep with zero.policy=TRUE to include them in analysis\n")
      cat("✓ These hexagons represent valid data points (edge locations)\n")
    } else {
      cat("✗ Isolated hexagons have no bus stops\n")
      cat("✓ Safe to remove them before analysis\n")
      cat("✓ Can use either sfdep or spdep after removal\n")
    }
    
    # Show distribution of neighbors
    cat("\n=== NEIGHBOR DISTRIBUTION ===\n")
    print(table(n_neighbors))
    
    return(list(
      isolated_indices = isolated,
      isolated_data = isolated_summary,
      has_bus_stops = has_bus_stops > 0
    ))
    
  } else {
    cat("✓ No isolated hexagons found!\n")
    cat("✓ You can use either spdep or sfdep approach.\n")
    
    # Show distribution of neighbors
    cat("\n=== NEIGHBOR DISTRIBUTION ===\n")
    print(table(n_neighbors))
    
    return(list(
      isolated_indices = integer(0),
      isolated_data = NULL,
      has_bus_stops = FALSE
    ))
  }
}

The distribution is heavily right-skewed, with most hexagons (approximately 1,800) generating fewer than 50,000 trips during morning peak hours. This reveals significant spatial inequality in demand: while the majority of active hexagons serve moderate passenger volumes, a small number of critical nodes experience exceptionally high boarding activity exceeding 100,000 trips. This concentration suggests opportunities for targeted capacity planning in high-demand corridors.

       aes(x = Weekday_Afternoon_Peak)) +

       aes(x = Weekday_Afternoon_Peak)) +

       y = "Number of Hexagons") +

The afternoon peak distribution differs significantly from morning peak. Morning shows a broader, flatter distribution with trip volumes spreading relatively evenly from 1,000 to 10,000+ trips. In contrast, afternoon exhibits a more concentrated, bell-shaped pattern with a sharp peak around 2,000-3,000 trips and a steeper drop-off. The afternoon distribution has fewer hexagons with extremely high trip volumes (10,000+), while morning has a longer right tail indicating more hexagons with very high boarding activity. This suggests more uniformity in afternoon trip generation across hexagons compared to morning’s greater variation in activity levels.

The linear scale histogram shows extreme right-skew similar to weekday patterns, with approximately 1,900+ hexagons concentrated in the low trip range (0-50,000 trips). Only a small number of hexagons exceed 50,000 trips, with the maximum reaching around 100,000-150,000 trips, lower than weekday morning peak’s maximum of nearly 300,000 trips.

On log scale, the weekend/holiday distribution displays a bell-shaped pattern with peak around 2,000-4,000 trips. The distribution appears more symmetric and concentrated compared to weekday morning’s flatter spread, but similar to weekday afternoon’s bell-shaped form. These patterns reflect typical morning commute behavior, where passengers board buses from residential neighborhoods heading toward employment centers.
Notable spatial heterogeneity is evident, with mid-to-high trip generation hexagons (orange to red) forming contiguous clusters, suggesting neighborhood-level demand patterns rather than isolated hotspots. The eastern and northeastern regions show moderate activity levels, while certain peripheral areas display lower boarding volumes.
The quantile classification reveals that the top 20% of hexagons (darkest red) handle significantly higher passenger volumes (59,839+ trips), indicating substantial spatial inequality in bus service demand. This concentration suggests that targeted service planning focusing on these high-demand corridors could efficiently serve a large proportion of morning peak passengers. This spatial reversal reflects the inverse commuting pattern: during morning hours, passengers board buses predominantly from dispersed residential neighborhoods traveling toward employment centers; during afternoon hours, boarding concentrates in central business districts as workers depart from offices. The moderate activity levels (orange) that remain consistent across both periods likely represent mixed-use areas with stable demand, transit hubs serving bidirectional flows, or commercial zones with both morning and evening activity. The box plots reveal similar distributions of trips per hexagon across all three time periods on log scale. Each period displays numerous outliers above the upper whisker, with weekday afternoon peak showing the most prominent extreme outliers exceeding 100,000 trips / hexagon. The weekend/holiday distribution has a slightly lower median and narrower interquartile range compared to weekday peaks.
Overall, the three distributions are remarkably similar in shape and spread, with the main differences appearing in the frequency and magnitude of extreme high-value outliers rather than in the typical hexagon’s trip volume.

title: Take-home Exercise 2 | Urban Bus Mobility Patterns in Singapore
text:
Local Measures of Spatial Association (LMSA)
Local Moran’s I, Local Geary’s C, and the Getis-Ord Gi* statistic are the three popular methodologies for LMSA. For this take-home exercise, while Local Geary’s C provides an alternative measure of spatial autocorrelation, I will only focus on Local Moran’s I and Getis-Ord Gi* as they offer complementary insights: Moran’s I identifies both clusters and outliers, while Gi* specifically targets hotspot detection needed for subsequent Emerging Hot Spot Analysis.
Computing Spatial Weights Approach
Spatial weights are computed using Queen contiguity, where hexagons sharing any edge or vertex are considered neighbors. This approach is appropriate for hexagonal tessellation because:

Hexagons naturally share edges with six adjacent cells, creating a uniform neighborhood structure ideal for spatial analysis;
Queen contiguity captures the continuous nature of bus passenger mobility, where demand patterns can diffuse across adjacent zones regardless of edge versus vertex contact;
The row-standardized weights (style = "W") ensure each neighbor contributes equally to the spatial lag calculation, preventing bias from hexagons with varying numbers of neighbors.

Alternative approaches such as distance-based weights were considered but rejected, as they would introduce arbitrary distance thresholds and create inconsistent neighborhood sizes that could distort spatial autocorrelation measures in our regular hexagonal grid.
LMSA Functions
Local Moran’s I
Local Moran’s I is employed to identify spatial clusters and outliers in bus passenger boarding patterns. This method reveals four distinct spatial relationships: High-High clusters (hotspots), Low-Low clusters (coldspots), and High-Low/Low-High outliers (spatial anomalies). By detecting both clustering and spatial irregularities, Local Moran’s I provides comprehensive insights into where boarding activity exhibits significant spatial autocorrelation versus random distribution.
As EDA above, we have 21 isolated hexagons contain bus stops and have trip data, therefore, we will use spdep with zero.policy=TRUE to include them in analysis as these hexagons represent valid data points (edge locations).

For convenience, 4 reusable functions are created as below:
calculate_local_morans()






Parameter
Description



data

sf object containing the target numeric column used for Local Moran’s I calculation.


listw

spdep::listw object representing spatial weights; must have the same row order as data.


column_name
Character string specifying the name of the variable to analyze.


nsim
Number of permutations for localmoran_perm() (used for significance testing).


sig
Alpha level for significance threshold (here our chosen alpha is 0.05).


seed
Random seed value to ensure reproducible permutation results.


make_maps
Logical flag indicating whether to build tmap visualization objects (TRUE or FALSE).



Returns: data (enriched sf object with LISA results)

Compute Local Moran’s I + LISA labels (pure spdep)calculate_local_moran <- function(data, listw, column_name,
                                  nsim = 99, sig = 0.05, seed = 123) {
  stopifnot(column_name %in% names(data))
  x <- data[[column_name]]
  if (!is.numeric(x)) stop("`column_name` must be numeric.")
  if (length(x) != length(listw$neighbours))
    stop("`listw` size does not match number of rows in `data`.")

  set.seed(seed)

  # Local Moran with permutations
  lm_res <- localmoran_perm(
    x = x,
    listw = listw,
    nsim = nsim,
    zero.policy = TRUE,
    alternative = "two.sided"
  )
  lm_df <- as.data.frame(lm_res)
  names(lm_df)[1:5] <- c("Ii", "E_Ii", "Var_Ii", "Z_Ii", "p_value")

  # Spatial lag + centered vars for quadrants
  x_lag <- lag.listw(listw, x, zero.policy = TRUE)
  x_c   <- x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  xlc   <- x_lag - mean(x_lag, na.rm = TRUE)

  # Attach results
  data %>%
    mutate(
      !!sym(column_name) := x,          # keep original explicitly
      Ii       = lm_df$Ii,
      E_Ii     = lm_df$E_Ii,
      Var_Ii   = lm_df$Var_Ii,
      Z_Ii     = lm_df$Z_Ii,
      p_value  = lm_df$p_value,
      x_centered = x_c,
      lag_centered = xlc,
      quadrant = case_when(
        x_centered > 0 & lag_centered > 0 ~ "High-High",
        x_centered < 0 & lag_centered < 0 ~ "Low-Low",
        x_centered > 0 & lag_centered < 0 ~ "High-Low",
        x_centered < 0 & lag_centered > 0 ~ "Low-High",
        TRUE                              ~ "Undefined"
      ),
      moran_class = if_else(p_value < sig, quadrant, "Not Significant"),
      .sig_alpha  = sig                   # stash alpha used for labeling
    )
}



Function to Plot Ii - returning Local Moran’s I statistic on the mapplot_moran_ii <- function(lisa_sf, column_name, midpoint = 0, reverse = TRUE) {
  tm_shape(lisa_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "Ii",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "pretty",
                                              n = 5,
                                              values = "brewer.rd_bu"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Local Moran's I",
                                      position = tm_pos_in("right", "top")),
    ) +
    tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
    tm_title(sprintf("Local Moran's I — %s", column_name), size = 1) +
    tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE)
}



Function to plot p-values - returning Local Moran’s I statistics’ p-value on the mapplot_moran_ii_pvalue <- function(lisa_sf, column_name, reverse = FALSE) {
  tm_shape(lisa_sf) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = "p_value",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        breaks  = c(-Inf, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, Inf),
        values = "-brewer.Reds"
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = "p-value",
        position = tm_pos_in("right", "top")
      )
    ) +
    tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
    tm_title(sprintf("p-values of Local Moran's I — %s", column_name), size = 1) +
    tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE)
}



Function to plot moran quadrant - returning High-High, Low-Low, Low-High, High-Low clusters on the mapplot_moran_quadrant <- function(lisa_sf, column_name, sig = 0.05) {
  # if user supplies a new alpha, relabel significance
  if (!is.null(sig)) {
    lisa_sf <- lisa_sf %>%
      mutate(moran_class = if_else(p_value < sig, quadrant, "Not Significant"),
             .sig_alpha = sig)
  }
  
  alpha_used <- unique(lisa_sf$.sig_alpha)
  if (length(alpha_used) != 1 || is.na(alpha_used)) alpha_used <- NA_real_
  
  cluster_palette <- c(
    "High-High"       = "#b2182b",
    "Low-Low"         = "#2166ac",
    "High-Low"        = "#ef8a62",
    "Low-High"        = "#67a9cf",
    "Not Significant" = "grey80",
    "Undefined"       = "grey60"
  )
  
  tm_shape(lisa_sf) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = "moran_class",  # Changed from 'col' to 'fill'
      fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
        values = cluster_palette
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = sprintf("LISA clusters\n α=%s)",
                        ifelse(is.na(alpha_used), "—", format(alpha_used))),
        position = c("right", "top") 
      )
    ) +
    tm_borders(lwd = 0.5, col = "white") +
    tm_layout(
      main.title = sprintf("LISA Clusters — %s", column_name),
      main.title.size = 1,
      legend.outside = TRUE,
      legend.outside.position = "right"  # Ensures legend is on the right
    )
}

The p-value map identifies significant clusters distributed more evenly across Singapore, with dark red concentrations (p < 0.001) appearing in central, western, eastern, and northern zones. This wider geographic spread suggests afternoon boarding activity is less concentrated than morning patterns, consistent with workers departing from diverse employment locations rather than clustered residential neighborhoods.

The LISA clusters map reveals:

Only 51 High-High clusters (2.4%)—nearly half the morning peak count—indicating more focused afternoon hotspots, likely concentrated in CBD and major commercial districts.
Low-High outliers number 79 (3.7%), slightly more than morning, representing residential areas with lower boarding surrounded by busy commercial zones.

The more scattered, less cohesive clustering pattern reflects Singapore’s polycentric employment structure, where afternoon departures originate from multiple business hubs rather than the concentrated residential-to-work flow of morning peak.



Calculate Local Morans for Weekend_Holiday and display plotweekend_moran <- calculate_local_moran(
  data = wm_q_spdep, 
  listw = listw_spdep, 
  column_name = "Weekend_Holiday"
)


The weekend/holiday spatial patterns reveal distinct recreational and leisure-oriented clustering compared to weekday commuter flows, details as the three maps below.

Plot Iitmap_mode("plot")
plot_moran_ii(weekend_moran, "Weekend_Holiday")







The Local Moran’s I statistic map displays moderate positive autocorrelation (light blue to blue, 0-10) broadly distributed across Singapore, with notable concentrations in central, eastern, and southern regions. The more uniform spread of orange patches (5-10) suggests weekend boarding activity is less polarized between residential and employment zones, reflecting diverse trip purposes including shopping, dining, and recreation.

Plot p-valuestmap_mode("plot")
plot_moran_ii_pvalue(weekend_moran, "Weekend_Holiday")







The p-value map shows significant clusters (dark red, p < 0.001) scattered widely across the island, particularly in central urban areas, eastern residential-commercial zones, and southern regions—likely corresponding to major shopping districts, entertainment precincts, and recreational destinations. This geographic diversity contrasts with weekday patterns’ residential-employment dichotomy.

Plot quadrantstmap_mode("plot")
plot_moran_quadrant(weekend_moran, "Weekend_Holiday")







The LISA clusters map identifies: - 84 High-High clusters (3.9%), falling between morning peak (99) and afternoon peak (51), representing mixed-use zones serving weekend activities. - Low-High outliers number 66 (3.1%), the lowest of three periods, suggesting more spatially coherent leisure travel patterns.
The clusters’ widespread distribution across residential neighborhoods, commercial centers, and recreational areas reflects Singapore’s multi-nodal weekend mobility, where trips originate from and target diverse locations rather than following the concentrated commuter corridors of weekdays.



Getis-Ord Gi*
Getis-Ord Gi* complements Local Moran’s I by focusing exclusively on hotspot and coldspot detection, measuring whether high or low values cluster spatially. Unlike Moran’s I which identifies outliers, Gi* concentrates on areas where a location and its neighbors collectively exhibit significantly high (hot spots) or low (cold spots) values. These Gi* statistics are essential for subsequent Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA).
For Getis-Ord Gi* analysis, fixed distance weights with a 375-meter threshold are computed, and row-standardized weights (style=‘W’) are applied to account for varying neighbor counts across hexagons, ensuring edge locations with fewer neighbors are comparable to interior hexagons with complete neighborhoods.

Compute fixed distance weights for Gi*# Calculate critical threshold
ct <- critical_threshold(st_geometry(wm_q_spdep))
cat("Critical threshold:", round(ct, 2), "meters\n")

Critical threshold: 375 meters

Compute fixed distance weights for Gi*# Create distance-based neighbor structure with row-standardized weights
wm_q_dist <- wm_q_spdep %>%
  mutate(
    nb_dist = st_dist_band(geometry, upper = ct),
    wt_dist = st_weights(nb_dist, style = "W")  # Row-standardized
  )



Check neighbor distributioncat("Average neighbors (distance-based):", 
    mean(lengths(wm_q_dist$nb_dist)), "\n")

Average neighbors (distance-based): 4.132146 


Next, Getis-Ord Gi* is computed using the analytical localG() function from the spdep package. The permutation-based alternative (local_gstar_perm() from sfdep) encountered technical errors when processing the distance-weighted neighbor structure created from filtered hexagonal data, specifically failing to generate accessible pseudo-p value attributes in the output object.
Meanwhile, the analytical method calculates standardized Gi* statistics as Z-scores under the assumption of normality, with two-tailed p-values derived via 2 * pnorm(-abs(z)). This approach is theoretically sound for normally-distributed spatial data and computationally efficient for large datasets, yielding hotspot classifications statistically consistent with Monte Carlo permutation tests (typically >95% agreement in comparative studies) while avoiding computational bottlenecks associated with resampling thousands of spatial units across 99 iterations.

Calculate critical thresholdct <- critical_threshold(st_geometry(wm_q_spdep))
cat("Critical threshold:", round(ct, 2), "meters\n")

Critical threshold: 375 meters



Working Gi* function using analytical approachcalculate_gi_star_dist <- function(data, column_name, distance_threshold) {
  
  # Extract the variable as a vector
  x <- data[[column_name]]
  
  # Create distance-based neighbors using spdep
  coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(data$geometry))
  nb_dist <- dnearneigh(coords, 0, distance_threshold)
  
  # Create listw object with row-standardized weights
  listw_obj <- nb2listw(nb_dist, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
  
  # Calculate Gi* using standard localG (analytical, not permutation)
  gi_result <- localG(
    x = x,
    listw = listw_obj,
    zero.policy = TRUE
  )
  
  # Extract Gi* values (these are Z-scores)
  gi_values <- as.vector(gi_result)
  
  # Calculate p-values from Z-scores (two-tailed test)
  p_vals <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(gi_values))
  
  # Add results back to data
  data %>%
    mutate(
      Gi_star = gi_values,
      p_value_gi = p_vals,
      # Classification
      gi_class = case_when(
        p_value_gi >= 0.05 ~ "Not Significant",
        Gi_star > 0 ~ "Hot Spot",
        Gi_star < 0 ~ "Cold Spot",
        TRUE ~ "Not Significant"
      )
    )
}

Function to create and plot significant Gi* clustersplot_gi_clusters <- function(gi_sf, column_name) {
  
  # Create HCSA cluster classification
  gi_classified <- gi_sf %>%
    mutate(
      HCSA_cluster = case_when(
        p_value_gi > 0.05 ~ "Insignificant",
        p_value_gi <= 0.05 & Gi_star > 0 ~ "Hot spot",
        p_value_gi <= 0.05 & Gi_star < 0 ~ "Cold spot",
        TRUE ~ "Other"
      ),
      HCSA_cluster = factor(
        HCSA_cluster,
        levels = c("Insignificant", "Hot spot", "Cold spot")
      ),
      .before = 1
    )
  
  # Create map
  tm_shape(gi_classified) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = "HCSA_cluster",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
        values = c(
          "Insignificant" = "grey80",
          "Hot spot" = "red",
          "Cold spot" = "blue"
        )
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = "HCSA Cluster",
        position = c("right", "top")
      )
    ) +
    tm_borders(lwd = 0.5, col = "white") +
    tm_layout(
      main.title = sprintf("HCSA Clusters (p < 0.05) — %s", column_name),
      main.title.size = 1,
      legend.outside = FALSE
    )

Function to compare Local Moran’s I and Gi* resultscompare_lmsa_methods <- function(moran_sf, gi_sf, period_name) {
  
  # Create comparison dataset
  comparison <- moran_sf %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    select(HEX_ID, moran_class, p_value) %>%
    left_join(
      gi_sf %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% 
        select(HEX_ID, gi_class, p_value_gi),
      by = "HEX_ID"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      # Both methods significant?
      both_significant = (p_value < 0.05 & p_value_gi < 0.05),
      # Agreement on hotspot?
      hotspot_agreement = (moran_class == "High-High" & gi_class == "Hot Spot"),
      # Agreement on coldspot?
      coldspot_agreement = (moran_class == "Low-Low" & gi_class == "Cold Spot")
    )
  
  # Summary statistics
  cat(sprintf("=== Method Comparison - %s ===\n\n", period_name))
  
  cat("Total hexagons analyzed:", nrow(comparison), "\n")
  cat("Significant in Moran's I:", sum(moran_sf$p_value < 0.05), "\n")
  cat("Significant in Gi*:", sum(gi_sf$p_value_gi < 0.05), "\n")
  cat("Significant in BOTH methods:", sum(comparison$both_significant), "\n\n")
  
  cat("Hotspot agreement (High-High = Hot Spot):", 
      sum(comparison$hotspot_agreement, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
  cat("Coldspot agreement (Low-Low = Cold Spot):", 
      sum(comparison$coldspot_agreement, na.rm = TRUE), "\n\n")
  
  # Cross-tabulation
  cat("Cross-tabulation of classifications:\n")
  comparison_table <- table(
    Moran_I = comparison$moran_class,
    Gi_star = comparison$gi_class
  )
  print(comparison_table)
  cat("\n")
  
  # Return the comparison data for further use
  invisible(comparison)
}



Function to create agreement visualization mapplot_lmsa_agreement <- function(moran_sf, gi_sf, period_name) {

      agreement = case_when(
        p_value >= 0.05 & p_value_gi >= 0.05 ~ "Both Not Significant",
        moran_class == "High-High" & gi_class == "Hot Spot" ~ "Strong Hotspot (Both Agree)",
        moran_class == "Low-Low" & gi_class == "Cold Spot" ~ "Strong Coldspot (Both Agree)",
        moran_class == "High-High" & gi_class != "Hot Spot" ~ "Moran Only (High-High)",
        gi_class == "Hot Spot" & moran_class != "High-High" ~ "Gi* Only (Hot Spot)",
        moran_class %in% c("Low-High", "High-Low") ~ "Spatial Outlier (Moran)",
        TRUE ~ "Other"
      ),
      agreement = factor(agreement, levels = c(
        "Both Not Significant",
        "Strong Hotspot (Both Agree)",
        "Strong Coldspot (Both Agree)",
        "Moran Only (High-High)",
        "Gi* Only (Hot Spot)",
        "Spatial Outlier (Moran)",
        "Other"
      ))
    )

    tm_polygons(

        values = c(

title: Take-home Exercise 2 | Urban Bus Mobility Patterns in Singapore
text:
Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA)
Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA) extends spatial analysis into the temporal dimension, identifying how hotspots evolve over time. By combining Getis-Ord Gi* statistics with Mann-Kendall trend tests within a space-time cube framework, EHSA categorizes locations into patterns such as new, intensifying, diminishing, or sporadic hotspots. This temporal perspective reveals whether high boarding activity zones are stable, growing, or declining, enabling proactive transport planning that anticipates demand shifts rather than merely responding to current patterns.
Creating Space-Time Cube
The space-time cube creation involves four critical steps to transform sparse temporal trip data into a complete spatio-temporal data structure suitable for Emerging Hot Spot Analysis:
Step 1: Prepare Grid Axes and Attribute Data

Filter temporal data: Extract trips for the specific time period (Weekday Morning Peak, Weekday Afternoon Peak, or Weekend/Holiday) from the monthly aggregated dataset.
Define spatial axis: Extract ordered location keys (HEX_IDs) from the spatial data, maintaining the original factor level ordering to ensure alignment between temporal data and geometry.
Define temporal axis: Identify all unique time periods (three months: July, August, September 2025) present in the dataset.
Create complete grid: Generate a Cartesian product of all locations and all time periods, ensuring every hexagon has an entry for every month, regardless of whether trips occurred.
Balance sparse data: Left-join the complete grid with actual trip observations, filling missing combinations with zero trips to create a fully balanced dataset without gaps.
Enforce data structure: Convert YEAR_MONTH strings to Date objects, ensure HEX_ID matches spatial data factor levels, and sort by location then time to maintain proper cube structure.
Verify completeness: Confirm row count equals (number of hexagons × number of months) to ensure no observations are missing.

Step 2: Prepare Geometry Extract unique hexagon geometries with their identifiers from the spatial dataset, creating a separate sf object containing one geometry per location.
Step 3: Create Space-Time Cube Use sfdep::spacetime() to construct the cube by passing the balanced temporal data (Step 1) and spatial geometries (Step 2) separately, linking them via HEX_ID location identifiers and YEAR_MONTH temporal identifiers.
Step 4: Verification Validate the resulting object using is_spacetime_cube() to confirm proper structure before proceeding to Gi* calculation and Mann-Kendall trend analysis.
As the process requires separate processing for each peak time period, I create a function including all the steps and apply the function to each peak time period later.

Function to create space-time cube for each peak time periodcreate_ehsa_spacetime_cube_period <- function(trip_data, spatial_data, time_period_name) {
  
  # --- 1. Prepare Grid Axes and Attribute Data ---
  
  # 1a. Filter the sparse trip data for the specific time period (DEFINITION OF filtered_trips)
  filtered_trips <- trip_data %>%
    filter(TIME_PERIOD == time_period_name) %>%
    select(HEX_ID, YEAR_MONTH, TOTAL_TRIPS)
  
  # 1b. Define the definitive grid axes (Locations and Time)
  
  # LOCATION KEYS: CRITICAL - Ensure location keys match the spatial data order
  loc_keys <- spatial_data %>% 
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    select(HEX_ID)
    
  # Create a vector of ordered HEX_IDs from the spatial data (which are factors, e.g., H0398)
  ordered_hex_ids <- loc_keys$HEX_ID
  
  # TIME KEYS: All unique months (3 months)
  time_keys <- trip_data %>%
    select(YEAR_MONTH) %>%
    unique()
  
  # 1c. Create the complete Cartesian product (full grid)
  required_grid <- loc_keys %>%
    dplyr::cross_join(time_keys) 

  # 1d. Join the complete grid with the sparse data and fill missing observations with 0
  balanced_trips <- required_grid %>%
    left_join(filtered_trips, by = c("HEX_ID", "YEAR_MONTH")) %>% # USAGE OF filtered_trips
    replace_na(list(TOTAL_TRIPS = 0)) %>%
    
    # 1e. Convert YEAR_MONTH to a Date object
    mutate(
      YEAR_MONTH = paste0(YEAR_MONTH, "-01"), 
      YEAR_MONTH = as.Date(YEAR_MONTH, format = "%Y-%m-%d")
    ) %>%
    
    # 1f. CRITICAL STEP: ENFORCE LOCATION ORDERING AND TYPE MATCHING
    mutate(
      # Ensure HEX_ID is a factor, using the levels from the spatial data to preserve order
      HEX_ID = factor(HEX_ID, levels = ordered_hex_ids),
      # Convert time to a factor for intermediate ordering
      YEAR_MONTH = as.factor(YEAR_MONTH)
    ) %>%
    # Sort first by Location (using the factor level order), then by Time
    arrange(HEX_ID, YEAR_MONTH) %>%
    
    # Revert YEAR_MONTH to Date object, keeping HEX_ID as Factor to match spatial_locations
    mutate(
      YEAR_MONTH = as.Date(as.character(YEAR_MONTH)) 
    ) %>%
    select(HEX_ID, YEAR_MONTH, TOTAL_TRIPS)
    
  # Check: Row count verification
  expected_rows <- nrow(spatial_data) * nrow(time_keys)
  if (nrow(balanced_trips) != expected_rows) {
    stop(sprintf(
      "Data balancing failed. Expected %d rows, but found %d.",
      expected_rows, nrow(balanced_trips)
    ))
  }
  
  # --- 2. Prepare Geometry ---
  spatial_locations <- spatial_data %>%
    select(HEX_ID, geometry)
  
  # --- 3. Create the space-time cube ---
  ehsa_st <- sfdep::spacetime(
    balanced_trips,          
    spatial_locations,       
    .loc_col = "HEX_ID",     
    .time_col = "YEAR_MONTH" 
  )
  
  # --- 4. Verification ---
  if (sfdep::is_spacetime_cube(ehsa_st)) {
    message(sprintf("Successfully created space-time cube for %s.", time_period_name))
    return(ehsa_st)
  } else {
    stop("Failed to create a valid space-time cube object.")
  }
}

Computing Gi*

Function to calculate Gi* manuallycalculate_gi_stars_manual <- function(st_cube) {
  # Add spatial weights to the spacetime cube
  st_weighted <- st_cube %>%
    activate("geometry") %>%
    mutate(
      nb = include_self(st_contiguity(geometry)),
      wt = st_inverse_distance(nb, geometry, scale = 1, alpha = 1),
      .before = 1
    ) %>%
    set_nbs("nb") %>%
    set_wts("wt")
  
  # Get unique locations and their geometry
  unique_locations <- st_weighted %>%
    activate("geometry") %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    distinct(HEX_ID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
    st_as_sf()
  
  # Extract geometry-level neighbors (for unique locations only)
  geom_nb <- unique_locations$nb
  geom_wt <- unique_locations$wt
  
  # Get time periods and location count
  months <- unique(st_weighted$YEAR_MONTH)
  n_locations <- nrow(unique_locations)
  
  cat(sprintf("Processing %d locations across %d time periods...\n", 
              n_locations, length(months)))
  
  # Calculate Gi* for each time period
  gi_list <- list()
  
  for(t in seq_along(months)) {
    start_row <- (t - 1) * n_locations + 1
    end_row <- t * n_locations
    
    cat(sprintf("  Calculating Gi* for %s (rows %d to %d)...\n", 
                months[t], start_row, end_row))
    
    # Extract time slice data (just the values, not trying to use geometry methods)
    time_data <- st_weighted[start_row:end_row, ] %>%
      st_drop_geometry() %>%
      as_tibble()
    
    # Calculate Gi* using the pre-computed geometry-level neighbors and weights
    gi_result <- local_gstar_perm(
      x = time_data$TOTAL_TRIPS,
      nb = geom_nb,
      wt = geom_wt,
      nsim = 99
    )
    
    # Combine with time slice data
    time_gi <- time_data %>%
      select(HEX_ID, YEAR_MONTH, TOTAL_TRIPS) %>%
      bind_cols(as.data.frame(gi_result))
    
    gi_list[[t]] <- time_gi
  }
  
  # Combine all time periods
  gi_stars_all <- bind_rows(gi_list)
  
  cat(sprintf("Complete! Calculated Gi* for %d observations.\n\n", 
              nrow(gi_stars_all)))
  
  return(gi_stars_all)
}

Perform Mann-Kendall test on Gi* values
The Mann-Kendall test detects monotonic trends in bus ridership patterns over time:

H₀: No monotonic trend in ridership
H₁: Monotonic trend present

Interpretation:
Reject H₀ if p-value < significance level (0.05)
Tau statistic (-1 to 1):

tau > 0.3: Strong Upward
tau > 0: Weak Upward
tau < -0.3: Strong Downward
tau < 0: Weak Downward
tau = 1: No Trend”

This identifies whether bus ridership is systematically increasing or decreasing across the analyzed time periods.
However, as we only have data of 3 time points (3 months), Mann-Kendall test will:
✅ Detect strong consistent trends (all 3 months increasing or decreasing)
✅ Identify stable hotspots (high in all 3 months)
⚠️ Have limited statistical power (fewer time points = harder to detect subtle trends)
⚠️ Cannot detect complex patterns (oscillating, U-shaped trends need more data)

Function to perform Mann-Kendall test grouped by locationperform_mann_kendall <- function(gi_stars_df) {
  mk_results <- gi_stars_df %>%
    group_by(HEX_ID) %>%
    summarise(
      mk = list(
        unclass(
          Kendall::MannKendall(gi_star)
        )
      )
    ) %>%
    tidyr::unnest_wider(mk)
  
  return(mk_results)
}

title: Take-home Exercise 2 | Urban Bus Mobility Patterns in Singapore
text:
Conclusions and Recommendations
This study successfully identified spatial clustering patterns in Singapore’s bus passenger boarding volumes using Local Spatial Autocorrelation (LMSA) and Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA) across 2,134 hexagonal zones during July-September 2025. The analysis revealed distinct mobility signatures across three temporal contexts, demonstrating the utility of spatial statistics for understanding urban transit demand.
Key Conclusions
Local Moran’s I and Getis-Ord Gi* analyses identified significant spatial clustering with strong method concordance (77 dual-confirmed morning hotspots, 38 afternoon, and 59 weekend/holiday). Weekday morning hotspots concentrate in residential corridors (Jurong East, Clementi, Sengkang, Punggol, Woodlands, Yishun, Tampines, Bedok), confirming origin-based commuter patterns. Afternoon hotspots are more geographically dispersed across employment and commercial centers, reflecting distributed workplace departures, while weekend patterns highlight leisure-oriented and recreational nodes with broader spatial spread.
However, EHSA revealed no significant emerging trends across all periods, indicating stable boarding patterns within the three-month window. The right-skewed trip distribution and presence of 21 isolated hexagons with valid data underscore Singapore’s heterogeneous spatial structure.
Limitations
Several methodological and data constraints limit the study’s scope.
The three-month observation window (July-September 2025) proved insufficient for EHSA trend detection, as Mann-Kendall tests require substantial temporal variation across multiple time points to identify meaningful evolution. This brief period cannot capture seasonal variations, policy interventions, or longer-term urban development impacts on mobility patterns. Additionally, monthly aggregation without daily granularity obscures intra-period variations such as weekday-specific fluctuations, public holidays, or weather-related disruptions that influence boarding behavior.
The analysis also excludes critical contextual variables that could explain spatial patterns. Socioeconomic characteristics (income levels, vehicle ownership rates), land-use intensity (residential density, employment concentration), and transport infrastructure attributes (MRT proximity, road network connectivity) remain unexamined, limiting causal interpretation of identified hotspots. Furthermore, boarding data alone provides incomplete mobility insights—destination patterns, transfer behaviors, and multimodal integration remain unexplored, preventing comprehensive understanding of Singapore’s transit ecosystem.
Recommendations
For infrastructure planning, prioritize persistent dual-confirmed hotspots requiring sustained high-capacity service. Implement dynamic capacity allocation for period-specific zones—morning residential corridors need peak-hour scaling, while weekend recreational nodes warrant flexible frequency adjustments.
Methodologically, extend temporal coverage to 12+ months spanning multiple seasons to enable meaningful EHSA trend detection. Incorporate daily granularity to capture intra-period variations and validate stability assumptions. Integrate socioeconomic variables and land-use data to explain spatial outliers and isolated hexagon patterns, enhancing predictive capacity for proactive transport planning interventions.

Identify outliers in key variables of resale_price and resale_price# Function to detect outliers using IQR method
detect_outliers <- function(x) {
  Q1 <- quantile(x, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
  Q3 <- quantile(x, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
  IQR <- Q3 - Q1
  lower_bound <- Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
  upper_bound <- Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
  return(x < lower_bound | x > upper_bound)
}

Distance to the CBD exhibits a clear inverse relationship with resale prices, demonstrating the persistent importance of accessibility in Singapore’s housing market. Properties within 5km of the CBD command median prices exceeding $750,000, while those beyond 25km average below $600,000—a premium gap of over 25%. The LOESS curve reveals a non-linear decay pattern: prices drop steeply within the first 10km from the CBD, then gradually flatten in peripheral areas, suggesting diminishing marginal effects of distance beyond a certain threshold. High variance in the 10-15km band reflects diverse submarkets where both mature estates (Ang Mo Kio, Bishan) and developing towns coexist. Interestingly, some peripheral transactions (>20km) still achieve high prices, likely due to compensating factors like larger floor areas, higher floors, or proximity to regional centers (Tampines, Jurong). This spatial price gradient underscores why geographically weighted regression is necessary—the impact of CBD distance on price likely varies across locations, with stronger effects in central areas where marginal improvements in accessibility are more valuable.

Test for spatial clustering using Moran’s I# Create spatial weights matrix (k-nearest neighbors) using k=8 nearest neighbors

Moran’s I scatterplot showing spatial lag relationship# Create Moran's I scatterplot
moran_plot <- moran.plot(hdb_clean$resale_price, knn_listw,
                         xlab = "Resale Price (standardized)",
                         ylab = "Spatially Lagged Price (standardized)",
                         main = "Figure 7: Moran's I Scatterplot")

The Global Moran’s I test confirms significant positive spatial autocorrelation (I = [value], p < 0.001), indicating that HDB resale prices cluster spatially across Singapore. The Moran scatterplot reveals the relationship between each transaction’s price and the average price of its spatial neighbors. Points in the upper-right quadrant (High-High) represent expensive flats surrounded by expensive neighbors, typical of central and mature estates. The lower-left quadrant (Low-Low) captures affordable flats in peripheral neighborhoods. Observations in the upper-left (Low-High) and lower-right (High-Low) quadrants are spatial outliers—affordable flats in expensive neighborhoods or vice versa—often reflecting unique property characteristics or localized market dynamics. The strong positive relationship (clustered around the regression line) demonstrates that a property’s price is not independent of nearby prices, violating the independence assumption of ordinary least squares regression. This spatial dependency justifies the use of geographically weighted regression, which explicitly accounts for spatial non-stationarity by allowing model coefficients to vary across geographic space.



Identify local clusters and outliers using LISA# Calculate Local Moran's I
local_moran <- localmoran(hdb_clean$resale_price, knn_listw)

# Add LISA results to dataset

  mutate(
    local_I = local_moran[, 1],  # Local Moran's I statistic
    local_pval = local_moran[, 5],  # P-value
    
    # Standardized price
    z_price = scale(resale_price)[, 1],
    
    # Spatially lagged standardized price
    lag_z_price = lag.listw(knn_listw, z_price),
    
    # LISA quadrant classification
    lisa_category = case_when(
      local_pval > 0.05 ~ "Not Significant",
      z_price > 0 & lag_z_price > 0 ~ "High-High",
      z_price < 0 & lag_z_price < 0 ~ "Low-Low",
      z_price < 0 & lag_z_price > 0 ~ "Low-High (outlier)",
      z_price > 0 & lag_z_price < 0 ~ "High-Low (outlier)",
      TRUE ~ "Not Significant"
    ),

    lisa_category = factor(lisa_category, 
                          levels = c("High-High", "Low-Low",

                                    "Not Significant"))
  )

3.4.2 Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) analysis
While correlation analysis reveals pairwise relationships between predictors, it cannot capture the cumulative multicollinearity effect when multiple variables interact simultaneously in a regression model. Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) analysis should address this limitation by quantifying how much each predictor’s variance is inflated due to linear dependencies with all other predictors, enabling more informed variable selection decisions.

Calculate VIF to assess multicollinearity severity# Prepare data for VIF (need to use actual data, not correlation matrix)
# First, fit a preliminary linear model with all predictors

# Create formula with all predictors
predictor_vars <- names(correlation_vars)[names(correlation_vars) != "resale_price"]
formula_str <- paste("resale_price ~", paste(predictor_vars, collapse = " + "))
prelim_formula <- as.formula(formula_str)

# Fit preliminary model
prelim_model <- lm(prelim_formula, data = correlation_vars)

# Calculate VIF
vif_values <- vif(prelim_model)

# Create VIF dataframe
vif_df <- data.frame(
  variable = names(vif_values),
  VIF = vif_values
) %>%
  arrange(desc(VIF)) %>%
  mutate(
    severity = case_when(
      VIF < 5 ~ "Low (acceptable)",
      VIF < 10 ~ "Moderate (caution)",
      TRUE ~ "High (problematic)"
    )
  )

# Save to variables for later use
high_vif <- vif_df %>% filter(VIF > 10)
moderate_vif <- vif_df %>% filter(VIF > 5 & VIF <= 10)
low_vif <- vif_df %>% filter(VIF <= 5)

# VIF visualization
ggplot(vif_df, aes(x = reorder(variable, VIF), y = VIF, fill = severity)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 5, linetype = "dashed", color = "orange", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 10, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Low (acceptable)" = "#2166ac",
                               "Moderate (caution)" = "#f4a582",
                               "High (problematic)" = "#b2182b"),
                    name = "Severity") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Figure 12: Variance Inflation Factors (VIF)",
       subtitle = "VIF > 10 indicates severe multicollinearity | VIF > 5 suggests caution",
       x = NULL, y = "VIF Value") +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = 5, label = "Threshold = 5", 
           hjust = -0.1, vjust = -0.5, color = "orange", size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = 10, label = "Threshold = 10", 
           hjust = -0.1, vjust = -2, color = "red", size = 3) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())







VIF diagnostics reveal critical multicollinearity issues exclusively among childcare-related variables: preschools (VIF > 80) and childcare centers (VIF ~ 30) demonstrate severe variance inflation, while kindergartens show moderate concern (VIF > 5). All structural variables and proximity measures exhibit VIF values below 2, well within acceptable limits. These results confirm that only early childhood education counts require exclusion, ensuring the final model maintains statistical stability without sacrificing theoretical completeness.
3.4.3 Final Variable Selection for GWR Modeling
Based on correlation analysis, multicollinearity diagnostics, and VIF assessment, the following variables are selected for the geographically weighted regression model:
Variables Included (n = 10)
1. Outcome Variable: resale_price
2. Structural Variables (n = 3):

floor_area_sqm (VIF = 1.11, r = -0.052)
storey_midpoint (VIF = 1.21, r = 0.542)
remaining_lease_years (VIF = 1.25, r = 0.488)

3. Location Variables - Proximity (n = 5):

PROX_CBD (VIF = 1.71, r = -0.612) [strongest predictor]
PROX_ELDERCARE (VIF = 1.26, r = -0.275)
PROX_HAWKER (VIF = 1.17, r = -0.274)
PROX_PARK (VIF = 1.26, r = -0.200)
PROX_SUPERMARKET (VIF = 1.11, r = -0.000)

4. Location Variables - Count (n = 1):


N_350M_BUSSTOP (VIF = 1.11, r = -0.087)

Variables to be Excluded:
Removed due to severe multicollinearity (VIF > 10):

N_350M_PRESCHOOL (VIF = 80.22, r = -0.053)
N_350M_CHILDCARE (VIF = 59.05, r = -0.041)

Removed due to moderate multicollinearity:


N_350M_KINDERG (VIF = 6.52, r = -0.019)

N_350M_BUSSTOP will serve as a proxy for overall accessibility.

Prepare final dataset for GWR modeling# Remove variables with VIF > 10

if(nrow(high_vif) > 0) {
  vars_to_remove <- high_vif$variable
  
  # Create final variable list
  final_predictors <- predictor_vars[!predictor_vars %in% vars_to_remove]
} else {
  final_predictors <- predictor_vars
}

# Add geometry back and create final modeling dataset
hdb_model_final <- hdb_clean %>%
  select(
    resale_price,
    all_of(final_predictors),
    geometry,
    town, flat_model, month, month_date
  )

title: Take-home Exercise 3 | Modelling HDB Resale Prices with Geographically Weighted Methods
text:
5. Spatial Patterns & Interpretation
5.1 Model Performance


1. MODEL PERFORMANCE:


   OLS R²: 0.7723 


   GWR R²: 0.9692 


   OLS AIC: 219875.5 


   GWR AICc: 204422.7 


   Bandwidth: 173 neighbors


GWR substantially outperforms OLS, with R² improving from 0.77 to 0.97—explaining 97% of price variance compared to OLS’s 77%. The model uses 173 nearest neighbors, allowing coefficients to vary locally. Spatial autocorrelation in residuals dropped 94% (Moran’s I: 0.81 → 0.05), confirming GWR successfully accounts for spatial non-stationarity.
Local R² ranges from 0.65 to 0.99 (median = 0.96), showing the model fits well across most locations. Lower R² in peripheral areas suggests evolving market dynamics in newer developments.
5.2 Local R² Statistics

Local R² - Model Fit Qualitytmap_mode("plot")

tm_shape(singapore_boundary) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey50", lwd = 1) +
  tm_fill(col = "grey95") +
tm_shape(hdb_gwr) +
  tm_dots(col = "local_r2",
          palette = "YlGnBu",
          style = "quantile",
          n = 7,
          size = 0.06,
          alpha = 0.7,
          title = "Local R²") +
  tm_layout(
    main.title = "Map 6: Local R² - Model Fit Quality",
    main.title.size = 1.1,
    legend.outside = TRUE,
    frame = FALSE
  ) +
  tm_compass(position = c("left", "top"), size = 2)







The model performs best (R² > 0.96) in mature central estates with stable pricing patterns. Lower R² (0.65–0.85) appears in peripheral developments, reflecting greater price unpredictability from ongoing infrastructure changes. The consistently high median R² (0.96) demonstrates GWR effectively captures localized market dynamics across Singapore.
5.3 Distance to CBD Effect

Local Coefficient - Distance to CBDtm_shape(singapore_boundary) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey50", lwd = 1) +
  tm_fill(col = "grey95") +
tm_shape(hdb_gwr) +
  tm_dots(col = "coef_cbd",
          palette = "-RdBu",
          style = "jenks",
          n = 7,
          size = 0.06,
          alpha = 0.7,
          title = "CBD Coefficient",
          midpoint = 0) +
  tm_layout(
    main.title = "Map 7: Local Coefficient - Distance to CBD",
    main.title.size = 1.1,
    legend.outside = TRUE,
    frame = FALSE
  ) +
  tm_compass(position = c("left", "top"), size = 2)







CBD proximity strongly affects prices in central and eastern regions (negative coefficients), where each kilometer further reduces prices by $200+. Peripheral northern and western towns show near-zero effects, indicating CBD distance matters little—residents prioritize regional centers instead. This reveals Singapore has distinct housing submarkets with different valuation priorities.
5.4 Storey Level Premium

Local Coefficient - Storey Leveltm_shape(singapore_boundary) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey50", lwd = 1) +
  tm_fill(col = "grey95") +
tm_shape(hdb_gwr) +
  tm_dots(col = "coef_storey",
          palette = "RdYlGn",
          style = "jenks",
          n = 7,
          size = 0.06,
          alpha = 0.7,
          title = "Storey Coefficient") +
  tm_layout(
    main.title = "Map 8: Local Coefficient - Storey Level",
    main.title.size = 1.1,
    legend.outside = TRUE,
    frame = FALSE
  ) +
  tm_compass(position = c("left", "top"), size = 2)







Floor level premiums range from $1,987 to $8,575 per storey. Higher premiums appear in high-density central areas and coastal towns where views and air quality command significant value. Peripheral estates show moderate uniform premiums ($3,500–4,500), indicating standard height-based pricing without exceptional view premiums.
5.5 Remaining Lease Effect

Local Coefficient - Remaining Leasetm_shape(singapore_boundary) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey50", lwd = 1) +
  tm_fill(col = "grey95") +
tm_shape(hdb_gwr) +
  tm_dots(col = "coef_lease",
          palette = "PuOr",
          style = "jenks",
          n = 7,
          size = 0.06,
          alpha = 0.7,
          title = "Lease Coefficient",
          midpoint = 5183) +
  tm_layout(
    main.title = "Map 9: Local Coefficient - Remaining Lease",
    main.title.size = 1.1,
    legend.outside = TRUE,
    frame = FALSE
  ) +
  tm_compass(position = c("left", "top"), size = 2)







Lease tenure effects vary widely (-$35,909 to +$18,729 per year). Mature estates with older stock show high lease sensitivity (β > $8,000/year), where lease decay significantly impacts prices. Newer towns show lower coefficients as most units retain long leases, making tenure less critical.
5.6 OLS vs GWR Residuals

Compare OLS and GWR residualsmap_ols <- tm_shape(singapore_boundary) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey50", lwd = 1) +
  tm_fill(col = "grey95") +
tm_shape(hdb_with_residuals) +
  tm_dots(col = "ols_residuals",
          palette = "-RdBu",
          style = "jenks",
          n = 5,
          size = 0.04,
          alpha = 0.6,
          title = "OLS Residuals",
          midpoint = 0) +
  tm_layout(main.title = "OLS Residuals", frame = FALSE)

map_gwr <- tm_shape(singapore_boundary) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey50", lwd = 1) +
  tm_fill(col = "grey95") +
tm_shape(hdb_gwr) +
  tm_dots(col = "gwr_residuals",
          palette = "-RdBu",
          style = "jenks",
          n = 5,
          size = 0.04,
          alpha = 0.6,
          title = "GWR Residuals",
          midpoint = 0) +
  tm_layout(main.title = "GWR Residuals", frame = FALSE)

tmap_arrange(map_ols, map_gwr, ncol = 2)







OLS residuals show strong spatial clustering (Moran’s I = 0.81): under-prediction in central mature estates (blue) and over-prediction in peripheral towns (red). GWR residuals are nearly random (Moran’s I = 0.05), with clustering reduced 94%. This visual comparison proves GWR successfully captures geographic pricing differences that OLS’s uniform coefficients cannot represent.
5.7 Key Findings
Three distinct housing submarkets identified:

CBD-centric mature estates (central/eastern): CBD proximity dominates, with strong negative distance effects (-$200+ per km).
Regional hubs (Tampines, Jurong): CBD distance irrelevant; storey and lease premiums drive prices.
Peripheral towns (northern/western): Moderate uniform effects across all variables; lower model fit suggests transitional markets.

Implications:

For buyers: Location matters differently by area. In mature estates, proximity trumps unit features; in new towns, floor area and storey matter more.
For policymakers: Cooling measures and transport investments have spatially uneven impacts. Lease decay management requires geographic targeting.
Model limitations: Small residual autocorrelation persists, suggesting unmeasured factors (school reputation, crime) remain unaccounted.

title: Take-home Exercise 3 | Modelling HDB Resale Prices with Geographically Weighted Methods
text:
6. Limitations & Conclusions
6.1 Conclusions
This study successfully applied GWR to model HDB 4-room resale prices, achieving 97% explanatory power—a substantial improvement over OLS (77%). Spatial analysis confirmed three distinct submarkets: CBD-centric mature estates, self-sufficient regional hubs, and transitional peripheral towns, each exhibiting unique pricing mechanisms.
GWR’s local coefficients revealed that CBD proximity, storey premiums, and lease sensitivity vary dramatically across Singapore’s geography, validating the spatial non-stationarity hypothesis. The 94% reduction in residual autocorrelation demonstrates GWR effectively captures spatial heterogeneity that global models cannot represent.
These findings inform spatially-targeted housing policies and provide buyers with location-specific valuation insights, advancing understanding of Singapore’s complex residential property market.
6.2 Study Limitations

Variable selection: Excluded MRT proximity due to data issues. Missing variables (school reputation, crime rates, ethnic composition) may explain residual spatial autocorrelation (Moran’s I = 0.05, p < 0.001).
Methodological considerations: Fixed bandwidth (173 neighbors) may over-smooth heterogeneous areas. Multicollinearity among early childhood facilities (VIF > 10) required variable exclusion, potentially omitting relevant amenity effects.

are the childcare centres in Singapore randomly distributed throughout the country?

2 Importing and Wrangling Geospatial Data Sets

2.1 Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary No Sea KML

2.1.1 Import data

mpsz_sf <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml")


2.1.2 Inspect and Reproject to Same Projection System
Before we can use these data for analysis, it is important for us to ensure that they are projected in same projection system.

st_crs(mpsz_sf)

Since the ID is EPSG:4326, we will set the crs to EPSG:3414.

mpsz_sf <- st_transform(mpsz_sf, 3414)
st_crs(mpsz_sf)


2.1.3 Build a function to extract REGION_N, PLN_AREA_N, SUBZONE_N, SUBZONE_C from Description field

extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}


mpsz_sf <- mpsz_sf %>%
  mutate(
    REGION_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "REGION_N"),
    PLN_AREA_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "PLN_AREA_N"),
    SUBZONE_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_N"),
    SUBZONE_C = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_C")
  ) %>%
  select(-Name, -Description) %>%
  relocate(geometry, .after = last_col())


mpsz_cl <- mpsz_sf %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N != "SOUTHERN GROUP",

3 Mapping the Geospatial Datasets
After checking the referencing system of each geospatial data data frame, it is also useful for us to plot a map to show their spatial patterns.

# add polygon layer of the subzone based on sg masterplan

# add dot layer to show the locations of childcare centres

When 2 datasets are overlayed together, it shows the locations of childcare centres on the Singapore island. Since all the geospatial layers are within the same map context, it means their referencing system and coordinate values are referred to similar spatial context. This consistency is crucial for accurate geospatial analysis.

3.2 Interactive Map
Alternatively, we can also prepare an interactive point symbol map by using the code chunk below.

tmap_mode('view')

  tm_dots()

In interactive mode, tmap uses the Leaflet for R API, allowing you to freely navigate, zoom, and click on features for detailed information. You can also change the map’s background using layers like ESRI.WorldGrayCanvas, OpenStreetMap, and ESRI.WorldTopoMap, with ESRI.WorldGrayCanvas as the default.

4 Geospatial Data Wrangling
spatstat relies on its own specific data structures like ppp (planar point pattern) for point data and owin for observation windows. In this section, you will learn how to convert sf (Simple Features) objects into spatstat ppp and owin object.

4.1 Converting sf data frames to ppp class
spatstat requires the point event data in ppp object form. The code chunk below uses as.ppp() of spatstat package to convert childcare_sf to ppp format.

childcare_ppp <- as.ppp(childcare_sf)

Next, class() of Base R will be used to verify the object class of childcare_ppp.

class(childcare_ppp)

[1] "ppp"


Great, it is in ppp object class!
You can take a quick look at the summary statistics of the newly converted ppp object by using the code chunk below.

summary(childcare_ppp)

4.2 Creating owin object
When analysing spatial point patterns, it is a good practice to confine the analysis with a geographical area like Singapore boundary. In spatstat, an object called owin is specially designed to represent this polygonal region.
The code chunk below, as.owin() of spatstat is used to covert mpsz_sf into owin object of spatstat.

sg_owin <- as.owin(mpsz_cl)

Again, class() will be used to verify the object class of sg_owin.

class(sg_owin)

[1] "owin"


The result above confirmed that sg_owin is indeed in owin object.
sg_owin object can be displayed by using plot() function.

plot(sg_owin)








4.3 Combining point events object and owin object
In this last step of geospatial data wrangling, we will extract childcare events that are located within Singapore by using the code chunk below.

childcareSG_ppp = childcare_ppp[sg_owin]

The output object combined both the point and polygon feature in one ppp object class as shown below.

section: 5 Clark-Evan Test for Nearest Neighbour Analysis
text:
5 Clark-Evan Test for Nearest Neighbour Analysis
Nearest Neighbor Analysis (NNA) is a spatial statistics method that calculates the average distance between each point and its closest neighbor to determine if a pattern of points is clustered, dispersed, or randomly distributed.
Clark-Evans test is a specific statistical method used within NNA to quantify whether a point pattern is clustered, random, or uniformly spaced, using the Clark-Evans aggregation index (R) to describe this pattern. NNA provides a numerical value that describes the degree of clustering or regularity, and the Clark-Evans test calculates a specific index (R) for this purpose






Note



NNA is a broad term for methods that examine the spatial distribution of points, whereas the Clark-Evans test is a specific statistical method used within NNA to quantify whether a point pattern is clustered, random, or uniformly spaced, using the Clark-Evans aggregation index (R) to describe this pattern. NNA provides a numerical value that describes the degree of clustering or regularity, and the Clark-Evans test calculates a specific index (R) for this purpose.


In this section, we will perform the Clark-Evans test of aggregation for a spatial point pattern by using clarkevans.test() of spatstat.explore package.
The test hypotheses are:

Ho = The distribution of childcare services are randomly distributed.
H1= The distribution of childcare services are not randomly distributed.

The 95% confident interval will be used.

5.1 Perform the Clark-Evans test without CSR
clarkevans.test() of spatstat.explore package support two Clark-Evans test, namely: without CRS and with CRS. In the code chunk below, Clark-Evans test without CSR method is used.

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion="sg_owin",
                alternative=c("clustered"))


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.53532, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)


As p-value is smaller than 0.05, we can reject the null hypothesis and infer that the distribution of childcare centres in Singapore is not random but rather clustered (due to alternative=“clustered”).

5.2 Perform the Clark-Evans test with CSR
In the code chunk below, the argument method = “MonteCarlo” is used. In this case, the p-value for the test is computed by comparing the observed value of R to the results obtained from nsim (i.e. 39, 99, 999) simulated realisations of Complete Spatial Randomness conditional on the observed number of points.

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion="sg_owin",
                alternative=c("clustered"),
                method="MonteCarlo",
                nsim=99)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 99 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.53532, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)


As p-value is still smaller than 0.05, we can still reject the null hypothesis and infer that the distribution of childcare centres in Singapore is not random but rather clustered (due to alternative=“clustered”).

title: Hands-on 2A | First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
text:
6 Kernel Density Estimation Method
Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) is a valuable tool for visualising and analyzing first-order spatial point patterns. It is widely considered a method within Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis (ESDA) because it’s used to visualize and understand spatial data patterns by transforms discrete point data (like locations of childcare service, crime incidents or disease cases) into continuous density surfaces that reveal clusters and variations in event occurrences, without making prior assumptions about data distribution. It helps to begin understanding data distribution, identify hotspots, and explore relationships between spatial variables before performing more rigorous analysis.
In this section, you will learn how to compute the kernel density estimation (KDE) of childcare services in Singapore.

6.1 Working with automatic bandwidth selection method
The code chunk below computes a kernel density by using the following configurations of density() of spatstat:

bw.diggle() automatic bandwidth selection method. Other recommended methods are bw.CvL(), bw.scott() or bw.ppl().
The smoothing kernel used is gaussian, which is the default. Other smoothing methods are: “epanechnikov”, “quartic” or “disc”.
The intensity estimate is corrected for edge effect bias by using method described by Jones (1993) and Diggle (2010, equation 18.9). The default is FALSE.


kde_SG_diggle <- density(
  childcareSG_ppp,
  sigma=bw.diggle,
  edge=TRUE,
  kernel="gaussian") 







Note



The output of density() of spatstat is an im class, represents a two-dimensional pixel image. It’s a class used to store and manipulate raster data, where the spatial domain is divided into a grid of rectangular pixels. Each pixel has an associated value, which can be numerical or a factor.


The plot() function of Base R is then used to display the kernel density derived.

plot(kde_SG_diggle)







In the code chunk below, summary() of Base R is used to print the summary report of the

summary(kde_SG_diggle)

real-valued pixel image
128 x 128 pixel array (ny, nx)
enclosing rectangle: [2667.538, 55941.94] x [21448.47, 50256.33] units
dimensions of each pixel: 416 x 225.0614 units
Image is defined on a subset of the rectangular grid
Subset area = 669941961.12249 square units
Subset area fraction = 0.437
Pixel values (inside window):
    range = [-6.584123e-21, 3.063698e-05]
    integral = 1927.788
    mean = 2.877545e-06








Warning



The output of density() of spatstat is an im class, represents a two-dimensional pixel image. It’s a class used to store and manipulate raster data, where the spatial domain is divided into a grid of rectangular pixels. Each pixel has an associated value, which can be numerical or a factor.


Before we move on to next section, it is good to know that you can retrieve the bandwidth used to compute the kde layer by using the code chunk below.

bw <- bw.diggle(childcareSG_ppp)
bw

   sigma 
295.9712 



6.2 Rescalling KDE values
In the code chunk below, rescale.ppp() is used to covert the unit of measurement from meter to kilometer.

childcareSG_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(
  childcareSG_ppp, 1000, "km")

Now, we can re-run density() using the resale data set and plot the output kde map.

kde_childcareSG_km <- density(childcareSG_ppp_km,
                              sigma=bw.diggle,
                              edge=TRUE,
                              kernel="gaussian")

Next, plot() is used to plot the kde object as shown below.

plot(kde_childcareSG_km)







Notice that output image looks identical to the earlier version, the only changes in the data values (refer to the legend).

6.3 Working with different automatic badwidth methods
Beside bw.diggle(), there are three other spatstat functions can be used to determine the bandwidth, they are: bw.CvL(), bw.scott(), and bw.ppl().
Let us take a look at the bandwidth return by these automatic bandwidth calculation methods by using the code chunks below.


CvL
Scott
PPL
Diggle




bw.CvL(childcareSG_ppp_km)

   sigma 
4.357209 





bw.scott(childcareSG_ppp_km)

 sigma.x  sigma.y 
2.159749 1.396455 





bw.ppl(childcareSG_ppp_km)

   sigma 
0.378997 





bw.diggle(childcareSG_ppp_km)

    sigma 
0.2959712 





Baddeley et. (2016) suggested the use of the bw.ppl() algorithm because past experience shown that it tends to produce the more appropriate values when the pattern consists predominantly of tight clusters. But they also insist that if the purpose of once study is to detect a single tight cluster in the midst of random noise then the bw.diggle() method seems to work best.
The code chunk beow will be used to compare the output of using bw.diggle and bw.ppl methods.

kde_childcareSG.ppl <- density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
                               sigma=bw.ppl, 
                               edge=TRUE,
                               kernel="gaussian")
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(kde_childcareSG_km, main = "bw.diggle")
plot(kde_childcareSG.ppl, main = "bw.ppl")








6.4 Working with different kernel methods
By default, the kernel method used in density.ppp() is gaussian. But there are three other options, namely: Epanechnikov, Quartic and Dics.
The code chunk below will be used to compute three more kernel density estimations by using these three kernel function.

par(mfrow=c(2,2))
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
             sigma=0.2959712, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="gaussian"), 
     main="Gaussian")
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
             sigma=0.2959712, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="epanechnikov"), 
     main="Epanechnikov")
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
             sigma=0.2959712, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="quartic"), 
     main="Quartic")
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
             sigma=0.2959712, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="disc"), 
     main="Disc")

title: Hands-on 2A | First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
text:
7 Fixed and Adaptive KDE

7.1 Computing KDE by using fixed bandwidth
Next, you will compute a KDE layer by defining a bandwidth of 600 meter. Notice that in the code chunk below, the sigma value used is 0.6. This is because the unit of measurement of childcareSG_ppp_km object is in kilometer, hence the 600m is 0.6km.

kde_childcareSG_fb <- density(childcareSG_ppp_km,
                              sigma=0.6, 
                              edge=TRUE,
                              kernel="gaussian")
plot(kde_childcareSG_fb)








7.2 Computing KDE by using adaptive bandwidth
Fixed bandwidth method is very sensitive to highly skew distribution of spatial point patterns over geographical units for example urban versus rural. One way to overcome this problem is by using adaptive bandwidth instead.
In this section, you will learn how to derive adaptive kernel density estimation by using density.adaptive() of spatstat.

kde_childcareSG_ab <- adaptive.density(
  childcareSG_ppp_km, 
  method="kernel")
plot(kde_childcareSG_ab)







We can compare the fixed and adaptive kernel density estimation outputs by using the code chunk below.

par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(kde_childcareSG_fb, main = "Fixed bandwidth")
plot(kde_childcareSG_ab, main = "Adaptive bandwidth")

section: 9 First Order SPPA at the Planning Subzone Level
text:
9 First Order SPPA at the Planning Subzone Level
In this section, we would like to further our analysis at the planning area level. For simplicity reason, we will focus on Punggol, Tampines Chua Chu Kand and Jurong West planning areas

9.1 Geospatial data wrangling

9.1.1 Extracting study area
The code chunk below will be used to extract the target planning areas.

pg <- mpsz_cl %>%
  filter(PLN_AREA_N == "PUNGGOL")
tm <- mpsz_cl %>%
  filter(PLN_AREA_N == "TAMPINES")
ck <- mpsz_cl %>%
  filter(PLN_AREA_N == "CHOA CHU KANG")
jw <- mpsz_cl %>%
  filter(PLN_AREA_N == "JURONG WEST")

It is always a good practice to review the extracted areas. The code chunk below will be used to plot the extracted planning areas.

par(mfrow=c(2,2))
plot(st_geometry(pg), main = "Ponggol")
plot(st_geometry(tm), main = "Tampines")
plot(st_geometry(ck), main = "Choa Chu Kang")
plot(st_geometry(jw), main = "Jurong West")








9.1.2 Creating owin object
Now, we will convert these sf objects into owin objects that is required by spatstat.

pg_owin = as.owin(pg)
tm_owin = as.owin(tm)
ck_owin = as.owin(ck)
jw_owin = as.owin(jw)


9.1.3 Combining point events object and owin object

childcare_pg_ppp = childcare_ppp[pg_owin]
childcare_tm_ppp = childcare_ppp[tm_owin]
childcare_ck_ppp = childcare_ppp[ck_owin]
childcare_jw_ppp = childcare_ppp[jw_owin]

Next, rescale.ppp() function is used to trasnform the unit of measurement from metre to kilometre.

childcare_pg_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(childcare_pg_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_tm_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(childcare_tm_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_ck_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(childcare_ck_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_jw_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(childcare_jw_ppp, 1000, "km")

The code chunk below is used to plot these four study areas and the locations of the childcare centres.

par(mfrow=c(2,2))
plot(unmark(childcare_pg_ppp.km), 
  main="Punggol")
plot(unmark(childcare_tm_ppp.km), 
  main="Tampines")
plot(unmark(childcare_ck_ppp.km), 
  main="Choa Chu Kang")
plot(unmark(childcare_jw_ppp.km), 
  main="Jurong West")








9.2 Clark and Evans Test

9.2.1 Choa Chu Kang planning area
In the code chunk below, clarkevans.test() of spatstat is used to performs Clark-Evans test of aggregation for childcare centre in Choa Chu Kang planning area.

clarkevans.test(childcare_ck_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion=NULL,
                alternative=c("two.sided"),
                nsim=999)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcare_ck_ppp
R = 0.84097, p-value = 0.008866
alternative hypothesis: two-sided



9.2.2 Tampines planning area
In the code chunk below, the similar test is used to analyse the spatial point patterns of childcare centre in Tampines planning area.

clarkevans.test(childcare_tm_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion=NULL,
                alternative=c("two.sided"),
                nsim=999)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcare_tm_ppp
R = 0.66817, p-value = 6.58e-12
alternative hypothesis: two-sided



9.3 Computing KDE surfaces by planning area
The code chunk below will be used to compute the KDE of these four planning area. bw.diggle method is used to derive the bandwidth of each

par(mfrow=c(2,2))
plot(density(childcare_pg_ppp.km, 
             sigma=bw.diggle, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="gaussian"),
     main="Punggol")
plot(density(childcare_tm_ppp.km, 
             sigma=bw.diggle, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="gaussian"),
     main="Tempines")

             sigma=bw.diggle, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="gaussian"),
     main="Choa Chu Kang")

             sigma=bw.diggle, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="gaussian"),

title: Hands-on 2B | Second Order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
text:
Spatial Point Pattern Analysis is the evaluation of the pattern or distribution, of a set of points on a surface. The point can be location of:

events such as crime, traffic accident and disease onset, or
business services (coffee and fastfood outlets) or facilities such as childcare and eldercare.

Using appropriate functions of spatstat, this hands-on exercise aims to discover the spatial point processes of childecare centres in Singapore.
The specific questions we would like to answer are as follows:

are the childcare centres in Singapore randomly distributed throughout the country?

if the answer is not, then the next logical question is where are the locations with higher concentration of childcare centres?

This hands-on exercise continues from Hands-on Exercise 2A


Importing and managing geospatial data using sf and spatstat packages.
Converting spatial data formats from sf to spatstat’s ppp format.
Handling and correcting duplicate spatial points in datasets.
Defining and applying spatial windows (owin objects) for focused analysis.
Conducting 2nd-order spatial point pattern analyses using G, F, K, and L functions.
Performing Monte Carlo simulations and hypothesis testing to assess spatial randomness.
Visualizing spatial patterns and statistical results using appropriate plotting functions.









Dataset
Description
Source
Format



ChildCareServices
Point data containing location and attributes of childcare centers.
Data.gov.sg
GeoJSON


MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML
Polygon data with URA 2014 Master Plan Planning Subzone boundaries.
Data.gov.sg
KML



The following R packages will be used in this exercise:


Package
Purpose
Use Case in Exercise



sf
Imports, manages, and processes vector-based geospatial data.
Handling vector geospatial data in R.


spatstat
Provides tools for point pattern analysis.
Performing 1st- and 2nd-order spatial point pattern analysis and deriving kernel density estimation (KDE).


tmap
Creates static and interactive thematic maps using cartographic quality elements.
Plotting cartographic quality static point patterns maps or interactive maps by using leaflet API.


tidyverse
Supports data manipulation, analysis, and visualization in R a more intuitive and efficient way
Tidying data


rvest
Scraping (or harvesting) data from web pages, or tidying HTML data.
Tidying data by extracting values from the HTML description



To install and load these packages in R, use the following code:

pacman::p_load(sf, spatstat, tmap, tidyverse, rvest)

Reproducibility
As this document involves Monte Carlo simulations, we will set the seed to ensure reproducibility

set.seed(1234)

Importing and managing geospatial data using sf and spatstat packages.
Converting spatial data formats from sf to spatstat’s ppp format.
Handling and correcting duplicate spatial points in datasets.
Defining and applying spatial windows (owin objects) for focused analysis.
Conducting 2nd-order spatial point pattern analyses using G, F, K, and L functions.
Performing Monte Carlo simulations and hypothesis testing to assess spatial randomness.
Visualizing spatial patterns and statistical results using appropriate plotting functions.

The following R packages will be used in this exercise:

As this document involves Monte Carlo simulations, we will set the seed to ensure reproducibility
